title: Data Types, Variables & Operators
relevance: Campus and SDE interviews probe C's type system, signed/unsigned conversions, operator precedence, and undefined behavior around side effects because these bugs dominate real C code.

phases.goal: Establish C's static scalar type system, size guarantees, fixed-width/alias types, and how literals and variables are typed.

must_hit.point: C is statically typed: every variable and expression has a type known at compile time, which dictates byte count and interpretation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states compile-time types decide size and how bits are read, not runtime discovery.

must_hit.point: The C standard guarantees minimum ranges for integer types, not exact byte sizes; the compiler picks sizes for the target hardware.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions minimum ranges vs exact sizes; may note int is at least 16 bits but typically 32 bits on modern systems.

must_hit.point: Integer types except char are signed by default; plain char signedness is implementation-defined, so use signed char or unsigned char for math.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Calls out char as the odd case and recommends explicit signed/unsigned char when behavior matters.

must_hit.point: sizeof reports size in bytes; <limits.h>/<float.h> expose actual min/max; <stdint.h> exact-width types (e.g. uint32_t) fix layout portability.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Distinguishes sizeof/limits from stdint exact-width and mentions int_fast*/int_least*/intptr_t family.

must_hit.point: size_t is the unsigned sizeof result type for sizes/indices; ptrdiff_t is the signed type from pointer subtraction.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses size_t for array indices/memory sizes and ptrdiff_t for pointer differences.

must_hit.point: Literals get types from syntax: integer default signed int (with U/L/LL suffixes), float literals are double by default (f/F for float), and in C a character literal has type int not char.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives examples like 42UL, 3.14f, and the C-vs-C++ char-literal type trap.

probes: What does C actually guarantee about the size of int versus types like int32_t?
Why is plain char special compared to other integer types?

hints.1: Think about what the compiler must know before runtime, and what the standard promises versus what hardware chooses.
hints.2: Separate minimum ranges, typical sizes, exact-width <stdint.h> types, and size_t/ptrdiff_t roles.
hints.3: Say: static types; min ranges not fixed sizes; char signedness is implementation-defined; use int32_t for exact layouts and size_t for sizes/indices; char literals are int in C.

phases.goal: Explain operators, short-circuiting, precedence, usual arithmetic conversions, and sequence-point rules for side effects.

must_hit.point: Logical && and || short-circuit: && evaluates the right side only if the left is true; || only if the left is false—used for NULL guards like ptr != NULL && ptr->value > 0.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains conditional right-hand evaluation and gives a safe pointer-guard pattern.

must_hit.point: Bitwise &, ^, and | bind looser than ==, so flags & MASK == 0 parses as flags & (MASK == 0); parenthesize as (flags & MASK) == 0.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Restates the precedence trap and the required parentheses.

must_hit.point: For binary operators, the compiler applies integer promotions then usual arithmetic conversions; same-rank signed+unsigned converts the signed operand to unsigned.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks promotions of char/short to int, then rank/signedness rules ending in signed-to-unsigned when ranks match.

must_hit.point: Example: int a = -1 compared with unsigned int b = 0 makes a > b true because -1 becomes UINT_MAX (typically 4,294,967,295) as unsigned.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Traces two's-complement all-ones reinterpretation and the true comparison result.

must_hit.point: A sequence point is where prior side effects are complete; modifying the same scalar twice without one (e.g. i = i++) is undefined behavior.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines sequence points and names i = i++ / a[i] = i++ style UB.

must_hit.point: Pre-increment (++x) yields the new value; post-increment (x++) yields the old value then increments; sizeof is compile-time except for VLAs.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts pre/post and notes sizeof's usual compile-time evaluation.

probes: Why can if (a > b) be true for int a = -1 and unsigned int b = 0?
What goes wrong with if (flags & MASK == 0), and how do you fix it?

hints.1: Mixed signedness and operator binding order are the two places C rewrites what you wrote.
hints.2: Name integer promotions, then usual arithmetic conversions; separately recall that == outranks bitwise &.
hints.3: Trace -1 to unsigned max before comparing; rewrite the bitwise test as ((flags & MASK) == 0); mention i = i++ as UB across sequence points.

phases.goal: Choose among int, fixed-width types, and size_t, and between #define and const, based on safety and intent.

must_hit.point: Use int when exact size does not matter (native efficient size); int32_t (etc.) for hardware/network/file layouts; size_t for memory sizes, byte counts, and array indexing.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Maps the three choices to generic counters, exact layouts, and size/index domains.

must_hit.point: #define is untyped textual replacement with no scope; const int gives a typed, scoped object the compiler prevents modifying after init.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts preprocessor text paste versus typed scoped const qualification.

must_hit.point: Widening casts (e.g. int to long long) are generally safe; narrowing (long to short, or float to int) truncates and can permanently change the value.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States widening vs narrowing risk and float-to-int fractional truncation.

probes: When should you pick int versus int32_t versus size_t?
What are the practical differences between #define MAX_USERS 100 and const int max_users = 100?

hints.1: Ask what property you need: native speed, exact width, or a size/index type.
hints.2: Separate value-domain choice (int/stdint/size_t) from constant definition (#define vs const).
hints.3: Answer with the interview triad: int for generic counters, int32_t for exact layouts, size_t for sizes/indices; prefer const for typed scoped constants over macros.

phases.goal: Apply type and operator rules to avoid UB and silent logic bugs in real code patterns.

must_hit.point: Uninitialized local automatic variables hold garbage; reading before writing is undefined behavior—locals are not zeroed by default.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States garbage contents and UB on read-before-write for block-scope autos.

must_hit.point: Loops comparing a signed int index to a size_t size can go wrong if i becomes negative: the comparison converts i to unsigned and may yield a huge value so the loop continues incorrectly.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Connects size_t return values to signed/unsigned conversion in i < size() style loops.

must_hit.point: In (int32_t)-5 + (uint32_t)10 then compare to uint64_t 2: -5 becomes 4,294,967,291 unsigned, plus 10 wraps to 5, then 5 < 2 is false (0).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Reproduces the worked trace: equal-rank signed→unsigned, wrap on add, then promote to uint64_t for the compare.

must_hit.point: Adding unsigned char 200 and 100 promotes both to int first, so the sum is int 300 and does not overflow an 8-bit unsigned char during the add.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says integer promotions widen before the add; result type int, value 300.

probes: What happens if you read a local int before assigning to it?
Walk through the type and value of (a + b) < c for int32_t a = -5, uint32_t b = 10, uint64_t c = 2.

hints.1: Look for uninitialized autos, mixed signed/unsigned compares, and small-type arithmetic that promotes.
hints.2: For the worked sum, apply promotions, then same-rank signed→unsigned, then rank-up to uint64_t.
hints.3: Locals start as garbage (UB if read); negative int vs size_t underflows in the compare; the -5/10/2 trace ends false; 200+100 as unsigned char becomes int 300.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: int for generic counters where exact width does not matter (compiler picks an efficient native size); <stdint.h> exact-width types like int32_t when modeling hardware, network packets, or file formats; size_t for memory sizes, byte counts, and array indices.
#define does untyped textual replacement before compile and ignores block scope; a const-qualified variable has a real type, respects scope, and cannot be modified after initialization.
Widening (e.g. int to long long) is generally safe; narrowing (long to short) drops high-order bytes and can change the value; casting float to int truncates the fractional part.

gotchas.trap: Assuming local variables start at zero
gotchas.correction: Automatic locals are not zero-initialized; they contain leftover garbage, and reading before writing is undefined behavior.

gotchas.trap: Writing if (flags & MASK == 0) for a bitwise test
gotchas.correction: == binds tighter than &, so it becomes flags & (MASK == 0); write if ((flags & MASK) == 0).

gotchas.trap: Expecting int a = -1; unsigned int b = 0; a > b to be false
gotchas.correction: Same-rank mixed signedness converts -1 to unsigned (UINT_MAX, typically 4,294,967,295), so the comparison is true.

gotchas.trap: Treating a C character literal like 'A' as type char
gotchas.correction: In C (unlike C++), character literals have type int.

gotchas.trap: Writing i = i++ or a[i] = i++
gotchas.correction: Modifying the same scalar twice with no intervening sequence point is undefined behavior; the compiler may do anything.

gotchas.trap: Relying on plain char for arithmetic signedness
gotchas.correction: Whether plain char is signed or unsigned is implementation-defined; use signed char or unsigned char explicitly when math behavior matters.
